chunks: My father narrated to us, may God be pleased with him, saying: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abdul Hamid ibn Awad al-Ta'i, who said: Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said:
Begging (al-mas'alah) is not proper except in three conditions: a large amount of blood-money (diyah), extensive debt, or extreme poverty.

key_terms.دَمٍ مُنْقَطِعٍ: A large or substantial amount of blood-money (diyah)

ai.seo_question: What are the three conditions under which begging is considered permissible in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: In *Al-Khisal*, Shaykh al-Saduq records Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) restricting the permissibility of begging (*al-musa'alah*) to three specific conditions: unpaid blood-money (*dam munqati'*), heavy debt (*gharam mu'thal*), or acute need (*hajjah mu'di'*). This hadith establishes a rigorous ethical framework in Shia jurisprudence, distinguishing between dignified necessity and habitual dependency, thereby preserving the social dignity of the beggar while ensuring aid reaches those with genuine, verifiable claims.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 3-148 (The compiler of the book narrated) that his father - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Sa’ed ibn Abdullah quoted on the authority of Ahmad ibn Aba Abdullah, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, on the authority of Hisham ibn Salim, on the authority of Abdul Hamid ibn Avaz al-Ta’ee that Abu Abdullah as-Sadiq (MGB) said, “
It is not proper to beg unless one is in one of three conditions: a large amount of blood-money, extensive debt or extreme poverty.”
